boxes.x: Definitions Sepsis = life-threatening organ dysfunction from a dysregulated host response to infection: SOFA rise ≥ 2 Septic shock = vasopressor to keep MAP ≥ 65 + lactate > 2 mmol/L despite adequate fluid (mortality > 40%) qSOFA (RR ≥ 22, altered mentation, SBP ≤ 100) = prognostic only; not a screening tool (SSC 2021) Exam opening ABCDE + "this is septic shock from an abdominal source: time-critical" Senior help, ICU, surgeon/IR early; parallel not serial actions State the definitions in one line each, then move straight to management.

Within 1 hour Lactate (repeat if > 2) Blood cultures before antibiotics (without delaying them) Broad-spectrum antibiotics 30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension or lactate ≥ 4 (SSC: "suggest", weak) Vasopressor if MAP  65 yr not worse) Lactate clearance or capillary refill time (ANDROMEDA-SHOCK: CRT-guided ≥ lactate-guided) Urine > 0.5 mL/kg/h, mentation Resuscitate to perfusion targets, not to CVP.

How much After initial bolus: give only if fluid responsive (PLR, PPV/SVV if ventilated, VTI change) CLOVERS (2023) & CLASSIC (2022): restrictive = liberal for mortality Watch for overload: rising FiO2, B-lines, VExUS congestion Which Balanced crystalloids preferred (SMART 2018: ↓ MAKE30; BaSICS & PLUS: no mortality difference) Saline: hyperchloraemic acidosis, possible AKI Albumin when large volumes needed (ALBIOS: no overall benefit; subgroup in shock) Avoid starches (6S, CHEST: AKI, RRT, death); gelatins not recommended Balanced crystalloid first, assess responsiveness before every further bolus.

Principles Identify source early: CT abdomen, US, line review Intervene within 6–12 h once resuscitated enough Least invasive effective option: percutaneous drainage > surgery when possible Remove infected devices (lines) after new access Examples Perforated viscus → laparotomy / laparoscopic washout Obstructed infected kidney → nephrostomy or stent Cholangitis → ERCP; necrotising fasciitis → radical debridement Antibiotics cannot sterilise an undrained source: say "source control within 6–12 hours".

Timing and choice Septic shock: within 1 hour (Kumar 2006: each hour delay ↑ mortality) Cover likely organisms + local resistance + risk factors (recent antibiotics, hospital, ESBL, MRSA, Pseudomonas) Abdominal: piperacillin-tazobactam or carbapenem ± anti-fungal if high risk PK/PD Loading dose regardless of renal function; ↑ Vd in sepsis Prolonged / continuous β-lactam infusion (BLING III 2024: ↓ mortality signal in meta-analysis) TDM for vancomycin, aminoglycosides, β-lactams Duration Short course after source control: STOP-IT (4 days ≈ longer) Procalcitonin to stop (SAPS, ADAPT-Sepsis): stop when ↓ ≥ 80% or < 0.5 µg/L; never to withhold initial therapy Daily de-escalation review "Hit hard and early, then de-escalate and stop early."

Sequence Noradrenaline first line; peripheral start acceptable short-term Add vasopressin 0.03 U/min when NA 0.25–0.5 µg/kg/min (VASST: NA-sparing; possible benefit in less severe shock) Adrenaline as second/third agent; angiotensin II (ATHOS-3) in refractory vasoplegia Cardiac dysfunction Echo: septic cardiomyopathy → dobutamine if low output despite MAP Levosimendan: no benefit (LeoPARDS) Steroids Hydrocortisone 200 mg/day if ongoing vasopressor (ADRENAL: faster shock reversal; APROCCHSS: ↓ mortality with fludrocortisone) Noradrenaline → vasopressin → hydrocortisone → echo-guided inotrope.

Metabolic resuscitation Vitamin C + thiamine + hydrocortisone: VITAMINS, VICTAS negative; LOVIT: harm with vitamin C Thiamine only if deficient (alcohol, malnutrition) Immunomodulation Sepsis endotypes (hyper- vs hypo-inflammatory), precision medicine IL-1 blockade in macrophage activation-like syndrome; GM-CSF / IFN-γ in immunoparalysis: research only Blood purification (CytoSorb, polymyxin B: EUPHRATES negative) Other Beta-blockade (landiolol STRESS-L: no benefit) Personalised MAP targets; early vasopressors (CLOVERS) Mention promising ideas but conclude "not recommended outside trials".

Structure (10 marks) Definition and severity → resuscitation targets → fluids (type/amount, evidence) → source control → antimicrobials (timing, PK, duration, PCT) → vasopressors/steroids → emerging → summary Numbers to quote MAP 65, lactate > 2, 30 mL/kg, 1 hour, 6–12 h source control, NA 0.25 µg/kg/min for vasopressin, hydrocortisone 200 mg/day Name a trial for every recommendation: examiners reward evidence.

Criteria Within 1 week of insult; bilateral opacities not fully explained by effusion/collapse Not fully explained by cardiac failure/overload (echo if no risk factor) PaO2/FiO2 with PEEP ≥ 5: mild 200–300, moderate 100–200, severe ≤ 100 2023 global definition Includes HFNO ≥ 30 L/min, SpO2/FiO2 ≤ 315, lung ultrasound in resource-limited settings Severe ARDS = P/F ≤ 100: say it, then escalate in steps.

Core Vt 6 mL/kg predicted body weight (ARDSNet ARMA 2000: mortality 40 → 31%) PBW male = 50 + 0.91 × (height cm − 152.4); female 45.5 + … Plateau ≤ 30 cmH2O; driving pressure ≤ 15 (Amato 2015: strongest predictor) Permissive hypercapnia, pH ≥ 7.20–7.25 SpO2 88–95% / PaO2 7.3–10.7 kPa Mechanical power Energy per minute (Vt, ΔP, RR, flow): lower is safer; avoid high RR 6 mL/kg PBW, Pplat ≤ 30, ΔP ≤ 15.

PEEP Higher PEEP in moderate-severe ARDS (ALVEOLI, LOVS, EXPRESS: meta-analysis benefit if P/F ART 2017: staircase RM + titrated PEEP ↑ mortality → avoid prolonged high-pressure RM Short RM only after disconnection/derecruitment Individualise PEEP; avoid routine aggressive recruitment (ART).

Evidence PROSEVA 2013: P/F < 150 (FiO2 ≥ 0.6, PEEP ≥ 5), early (< 36 h), ≥ 16 h/day → 28-day mortality 33 → 16% Practice Trained team, pressure areas, ETT/line safety, eyes, enteral feed Stop when P/F ≥ 150 with PEEP ≤ 10, FiO2 ≤ 0.6 for 4 h after supine Contraindications: unstable spine, open abdomen, raised ICP (relative), pregnancy (relative, feasible) Prone early and long: PROSEVA is the single most important ARDS trial to quote.

NMB ACURASYS 2010: cisatracurium 48 h ↓ mortality; ROSE 2019: no benefit with lighter sedation and higher PEEP Use for dyssynchrony, high Pplat despite sedation, during proning Inhaled NO / prostacyclin Improve oxygenation transiently; no survival benefit, ↑ AKI with NO Rescue bridge to prone/ECMO, or RV failure Steroids Dexamethasone (DEXA-ARDS) for moderate-severe ARDS; COVID-19 (RECOVERY); CAP (CAPE COD hydrocortisone) Oxygenation improvement does not mean survival benefit.

Referral criteria (EOLIA) P/F  3 h, or  6 h pH  6 h (RR 35, Pplat ≤ 32) Despite optimal care incl. prone and NMB Evidence CESAR 2009: referral to ECMO centre ↓ death/disability EOLIA 2018: 35% vs 46% (NS), but crossover 28%; Bayesian and meta-analysis favour ECMO Contraindications Ventilated > 7 days with high settings (relative), irreversible disease, severe immunosuppression, contraindication to anticoagulation Refer early to a high-volume centre; ECMO is a bridge, not a cure.

Mortality predictors Age, severity (P/F), driving pressure, dead space fraction, non-pulmonary organ failure, immunosuppression RESP score (ECMO survival), PRESERVE score Ethics Resource allocation, candidacy, bridge to nowhere, family communication, time-limited trial, withdrawal on ECMO Finish the answer with prognosis and an ethical sentence.

HFNO / NIV FLORALI: HFNO ↓ intubation in P/F ≤ 200 and ↓ mortality vs NIV/O2 Watch HACOR score / ROX index; avoid delayed intubation and P-SILI Cause-specific CAP: early antibiotics, steroids (CAPE COD) in severe CAP Influenza: oseltamivir; COVID-19: dexamethasone, IL-6 blockade Conservative fluid strategy once shock resolved (FACTT) Treat the cause while protecting the lung.

Readiness Cause improving, P/F > 150–200 on PEEP ≤ 8, FiO2 ≤ 0.4–0.5 Haemodynamically stable (little or no vasopressor), awake (RASS 0/−1), cough, manageable secretions SBT 30–120 min T-piece or PSV 5–8 / PEEP 0–5 Failure: RR > 35, SpO2  140 or ↑ 20%, SBP > 180 or  7 days) Daily screen + daily SBT + paired sedation hold (ABC trial).

Load vs capacity Airway/lung: secretions, bronchospasm, ↑ resistance, PEEPi (COPD), effusion, oedema Brain: delirium, sedation, anxiety/psychological dependence Cardiac: weaning-induced pulmonary oedema (ischaemia, LV dysfunction) Diaphragm: ventilator-induced diaphragm dysfunction, phrenic injury, ICU-AW, electrolytes (↓ PO4, K, Mg), hypothyroid Endocrine/metabolic: metabolic alkalosis, nutrition, anaemia Frame it as respiratory load versus neuromuscular capacity, plus cardiac and psychological.

Mechanism Negative pleural pressure ↑ venous return and LV afterload; catecholamine surge; ischaemia Diagnosis Rise in Hb/protein > 5–6% during SBT, BNP rise, echo E/e′ ↑, lung US B-lines, PAOP > 18 Treatment Diuretics, nitrates, ischaemia treatment; extubate to NIV Suspect it in COPD + heart disease who fails within minutes with hypertension.

ICU-AW Critical illness polyneuropathy/myopathy; MRC sum score < 48 Risks: sepsis, MOF, hyperglycaemia, steroids, NMB, immobility Nerve conduction/EMG if atypical; exclude GBS, myasthenia, cord lesion Diaphragm Ultrasound: thickening fraction < 20–30% or excursion < 1 cm = dysfunction Avoid over-assistance and over-sedation; inspiratory muscle training Management Early mobilisation, glucose control, minimise steroids/NMB, nutrition, physiotherapy Prevention beats treatment: light sedation and early mobilisation.

T-piece Closest to post-extubation work of breathing; unmasks cardiac failure Higher failure rate, may delay extubation PSV 5–8 Easier, compensates tube resistance (but upper airway oedema after extubation adds similar load) Subirà 2019 (JAMA): 30 min PSV 8 → more successful extubation than 2 h T-piece After extubation (high risk) NIV or HFNO+NIV (HIGH-WEAN) for > 65 yr, heart failure, COPD, obesity Cuff leak test in high-risk for stridor → steroids 12–24 h before Choose PSV for most; T-piece when cardiac failure is suspected.

Benefits Less sedation, comfort, oral hygiene, ↓ dead space and resistance, easier weaning and mobilisation, ward discharge Timing TracMan 2013: early (day 1–4) vs late (≥ day 10) → no mortality difference; 45% of late group never needed one Consider after ~10 days if weaning not imminent; earlier in neuro injury (SETPOINT2: no outcome benefit) Technique and risks Percutaneous dilatational (bronchoscopy, US) vs surgical Bleeding, loss of airway, stenosis; NTSP safety bundles Tracheostomy does not cut mortality; it facilitates weaning.

Steps Identify and treat each cause; daily SBT or progressive reduction of PSV Tracheostomy mask trials (↑ duration), night rest on ventilator Specialised weaning unit, home NIV for hypercapnic COPD Systematic: diagnose, correct, retest, rehabilitate.

Steps pH → primary process (HCO3 / PaCO2) Compensation: Winter: expected PaCO2 = 1.5 × HCO3 + 8 (± 2) mmHg Anion gap = Na − (Cl + HCO3), normal 8–12; correct for albumin: +2.5 per 10 g/L below 40 Delta ratio (ΔAG/ΔHCO3):  2 + metabolic alkalosis Osmolar gap = measured − (2Na + glucose + urea), > 10 abnormal Always correct the anion gap for albumin in ICU patients.

GOLDMARK Glycols (ethylene, propylene) Oxoproline (pyroglutamic acid) L-lactate D-lactate (short bowel) Methanol Aspirin Renal failure Ketoacidosis (diabetic, alcoholic, starvation) In pancreatitis + alcohol Lactate (shock, ischaemia), AKA, AKI, toxic alcohol co-ingestion, thiamine deficiency Use GOLDMARK and then point to the likely ones in the stem.

boxes.t: 3. Type A vs Type B lactic acidosis
boxes.x: Type A (hypoperfusion/hypoxia) Shock, regional ischaemia (mesenteric), severe hypoxaemia, anaemia, CO poisoning Type B (no hypoperfusion) B1 disease: liver failure, sepsis (aerobic glycolysis, β2 stimulation), malignancy, thiamine deficiency B2 drugs: metformin, adrenaline, salbutamol, propofol infusion syndrome, linezolid, NRTIs, cyanide (nitroprusside) B3 inborn errors How to separate Perfusion markers (CRT, ScvO2, CO2 gap > 6 mmHg), lactate/pyruvate, response to resuscitation, drug history A lactate that does not fall with resuscitation: think Type B or hidden ischaemia.

Steps Treat the cause: resuscitate, source control, stop offending drugs, thiamine Ventilation: match respiratory compensation if intubated (avoid ↓ minute volume) Vasopressors for shock (catecholamine response falls at pH BICAR-ICU 2018: no overall benefit; pH ≤ 7.20 + AKI (KDIGO 2–3) → ↓ mortality and RRT Indicated: NAGMA with bicarbonate loss, hyperkalaemia, TCA/salicylate toxicity RRT Refractory acidosis, AKI, toxins (dialysable) Quote BICAR-ICU: bicarbonate helps in pH ≤ 7.2 with AKI.

Pyroglutamic (5-oxoproline) Glutathione depletion: chronic paracetamol + sepsis, malnutrition, liver/renal disease, flucloxacillin, vigabatrin; women HAGMA without lactate/ketones/toxic alcohol; urine organic acids (5-oxoproline) Stop paracetamol and flucloxacillin, give N-acetylcysteine Propylene glycol Solvent in IV lorazepam, diazepam, phenobarbital, etomidate High doses → HAGMA, raised osmolar gap, lactate (metabolised to L-lactate), AKI Monitor osmolar gap (> 10–12) in prolonged high-dose lorazepam; stop drug, RRT if severe Unexplained HAGMA in ICU: check osmolar gap and drug chart.

Features Early ↑ osmolar gap → later ↑ anion gap Ethylene glycol: oxalate crystals, AKI, hypocalcaemia Methanol: visual loss, basal ganglia necrosis Treatment Fomepizole (or ethanol) to block alcohol dehydrogenase Haemodialysis (EXTRIP): severe acidosis, AKI, visual signs, high level Cofactors: thiamine + pyridoxine (EG), folinic acid (methanol); bicarbonate High AG + high osmolar gap = toxic alcohol until proven otherwise.

KDIGO Stage 1: Cr × 1.5–1.9 or ↑ 26.5 µmol/L; UO < 0.5 mL/kg/h 6–12 h Stage 2: × 2–2.9; stage 3: × 3, Cr ≥ 354, RRT, UO < 0.3 × 24 h or anuria 12 h RRT timing and dose STARRT-AKI, AKIKI: early start no benefit; start for life-threatening indications (AEIOU) Dose 20–25 mL/kg/h effluent (RENAL, ATN) Citrate anticoagulation preferred for CRRT No benefit from accelerated RRT: wait for a clear indication.

Limitations Static pressure ≠ volume; poor predictor of fluid responsiveness (Marik 2013: AUC ≈ 0.56) Affected by RV function, tricuspid disease, PEEP, intra-abdominal pressure, compliance, tamponade High CVP (e.g. 16) with oliguria → venous congestion lowers renal perfusion pressure (MAP − CVP) Where CVP helps Trend, RV failure, tamponade, safety ceiling for fluids, ScvO2 sampling, waveform (cannon a, large v) "CVP tells you about the right heart and congestion, not about fluid need."

Dynamic tests Passive leg raise: ↑ CO/VTI ≥ 10% (works in AF, spontaneous breathing) PPV/SVV > 12–13% only if ventilated Vt ≥ 8, sinus rhythm, closed chest, no spontaneous effort End-expiratory occlusion (↑ CO ≥ 5%), mini-fluid challenge 100 mL, tidal volume challenge IVC variability (limited; spontaneous breathing unreliable) Responsive ≠ needs fluid: give only if responsive AND hypoperfused.

Pulse contour (FloTrac, LiDCO, PiCCO) Continuous CO and SVV; uncalibrated less accurate in vasoplegia, arrhythmia, IABP, poor arterial trace Transpulmonary thermodilution (PiCCO, VolumeView) Calibrated CO, GEDV (preload), EVLW (oedema), PVPI; needs central line + femoral arterial; recalibrate Pulmonary artery catheter CO, PAOP, PAP, SvO2, PVR; RV failure, pulmonary hypertension, cardiac surgery PAC-Man 2005: no mortality benefit; complications Echocardiography Diagnosis: LV/RV function, tamponade, valves, LVOT obstruction (SAM), VTI Operator-dependent, intermittent; TOE after cardiac surgery Echo to diagnose, a continuous CO monitor to titrate.

Patterns LV failure: ↓ CO/CI  18, ↑ SVR, ↓ SvO2; echo poor LVEF RV failure: ↑ CVP > PAOP, dilated RV, D-shaped septum, TAPSE Tamponade: equalised pressures, collapsing RA/RV, low CO; localised clot after surgery Vasoplegia: normal/↑ CO, ↓ SVR Hypovolaemia: ↓ CO, small hyperdynamic LV, responsive to PLR Name the phenotype, then match the drug to the problem.

LV failure Optimise preload, inotrope (dobutamine/milrinone), noradrenaline for MAP, reduce afterload when MAP allows Mechanical support: IABP (IABP-SHOCK II: no benefit in MI), Impella, VA-ECMO (ECLS-SHOCK: no benefit routinely) RV failure Avoid overload; maintain MAP > PAP (noradrenaline, vasopressin) Milrinone/dobutamine, inhaled NO/epoprostenol, lower PEEP/plateau, correct hypoxia, hypercapnia, acidosis Tamponade Re-sternotomy (cardiac surgery) or pericardiocentesis; keep preload and HR, avoid high PEEP RV failure: "pressure up, pulmonary resistance down, avoid fluids".

Causes Bleeding/hypovolaemia, tamponade, LV/RV dysfunction (stunning, graft failure), valve dysfunction/SAM after MV repair, vasoplegia, arrhythmia, pacing problems Actions Check drains, ROTEM, echo (TOE), ECG, pacing wires (AV pacing 90) Methylene blue for refractory vasoplegia; CALS for arrest (resternotomy < 5 min) After cardiac surgery: think bleeding and tamponade first.

SCAI stages A at risk, B beginning, C classic, D deteriorating, E extremis Key steps Early revascularisation of culprit lesion (SHOCK trial); culprit-only PCI (CULPRIT-SHOCK) Lactate and end-organ monitoring; shock team; noradrenaline > dopamine (SOAP II) Revascularise early, support wisely, avoid routine mechanical devices.

Example: PT 35 s, aPTT 55 s, fibrinogen 0.8, platelets 45, D-dimer > 20,000 Consumption + dilution + liver synthetic failure Low fibrinogen + very high D-dimer + oozing from lines → DIC and/or hyperfibrinolysis on background of cirrhosis Rebalanced haemostasis in cirrhosis ↓ pro- and anticoagulant factors (protein C, AT); ↑ factor VIII and vWF INR does not predict bleeding; global tests (TEG/ROTEM) better Do not treat the INR; treat bleeding guided by global tests.

boxes.t: 2. Liver disease vs DIC vs hyperfibrinolysis
boxes.x: Liver disease Normal/↑ factor VIII, low factor V and VII, stable picture, splenomegaly-related thrombocytopenia DIC ISTH score ≥ 5 (platelets, D-dimer/FDP, PT, fibrinogen); trigger (sepsis, shock, trauma) ↓ factor VIII (consumed), falling platelets and fibrinogen over time, schistocytes Hyperfibrinolysis Very low fibrinogen, very high D-dimer, oozing; ROTEM: ML > 15% in EXTEM, corrected by APTEM; euglobulin lysis time short Factor VIII separates them: high in liver disease, low in DIC.

General Control the source (endoscopy, TIPS, surgery), warm, Ca2+ > 1.1, pH > 7.2 Restrictive transfusion Hb 70 g/L in variceal bleeding (Villanueva 2013 ↓ mortality) Targets Fibrinogen > 1.5 g/L (> 2 in obstetric): cryoprecipitate 10 units or concentrate 3–4 g Platelets > 50 ×10⁹/L if bleeding (> 100 for neurosurgery) FFP: only if ROTEM CT prolonged or active bleeding with ↑ PT; volume overload ↑ portal pressure Tranexamic acid for hyperfibrinolysis (HALT-IT: no benefit in GI bleed and ↑ VTE) Give the specific product for the specific defect.

Steps Terlipressin/octreotide, antibiotics (ceftriaxone), endoscopic band ligation < 12 h Airway protection; restrictive transfusion Pre-emptive TIPS (< 72 h) in Child C 10–13 or B with active bleed (Baveno VII) Balloon tamponade/esophageal stent as bridge Vasoactive drug + antibiotics + early banding + consider early TIPS.

Evidence Variceal bleeding (Bosch 2004, 2008): no benefit overall Trauma (CONTROL): ↓ transfusion, no mortality benefit Off-label use ↑ arterial thrombosis (Levi 2010 NEJM) If used Last resort after surgical control and correction of fibrinogen, platelets, Ca, pH, temperature Not recommended routinely: thrombosis risk without survival benefit.

Reading ROTEM CT (clotting time) ↑ → factors → FFP/PCC A5/A10 FIBTEM  15% → antifibrinolytic HEPTEM vs INTEM → heparin effect Evidence Cirrhosis procedures: TEG-guided ↓ products without more bleeding (De Pietri 2016) Cardiac surgery and trauma: ↓ transfusion Limitations Insensitive to antiplatelet drugs, vWF, hypothermia (run at 37 °C) Fast, global, guides products: but treat the patient, not the trace.

Key points RBC:FFP:platelets ≈ 1:1:1 until results (PROPPR) TXA 1 g within 3 h in trauma (CRASH-2) and PPH (WOMAN) Permissive hypotension in trauma (not TBI) Monitor Ca, K, temperature, lactate; avoid > 2 L crystalloid Activate early, balanced products, then switch to goal-directed.

ILAE 2015 t1 = 5 min (treat), t2 = 30 min (risk of damage) for convulsive SE Established SE: fails benzodiazepines Refractory: fails benzodiazepine + one second-line drug Super-refractory: continues ≥ 24 h after anaesthetic or recurs on weaning Time is brain: every step has a time target.

Doses Lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg IV (4 mg), repeat once Midazolam 10 mg IM/buccal (RAMPART: IM midazolam ≥ IV lorazepam pre-hospital) Diazepam 10 mg IV Pitfalls Under-dosing is common; ABC, glucose (thiamine first if malnourished), check airway Adequate benzodiazepine dose, then move on within 10 minutes.

ESETT 2019 Levetiracetam 60 mg/kg (max 4.5 g), fosphenytoin 20 mg PE/kg, valproate 40 mg/kg (max 3 g): equal efficacy ≈ 47% Choice Levetiracetam: few interactions; adjust in renal failure Phenytoin: arrhythmia, hypotension, purple glove; monitor ECG; level Valproate: avoid in liver disease, mitochondrial disease, pregnancy; hyperammonaemia; levels Lacosamide 200–400 mg: PR prolongation; phenobarbital 15–20 mg/kg No winner in ESETT: choose by comorbidity and side-effects.

Agents Midazolam 0.2 mg/kg then 0.05–2 mg/kg/h: tachyphylaxis Propofol 1–2 mg/kg then 2–10 mg/kg/h: PRIS (keep Ketamine (NMDA): useful later when GABA receptors internalised; haemodynamically stable Thiopental/pentobarbital: hypotension, immunosuppression, long half-life Goals Continuous EEG: seizure suppression or burst suppression for 24–48 h, then slow wean Intubation, vasopressors, temperature control Balance seizure control against deep sedation harms: aim for the least EEG suppression that works.

Options Ketamine, ketogenic diet, immunotherapy (steroids, IVIG, plasma exchange, rituximab), magnesium, pyridoxine in children Hypothermia (HYBERNATUS: no outcome benefit), surgery for focus, ECT NORSE / FIRES New-onset refractory SE without clear cause; autoimmune encephalitis (NMDA-R) common Early first-line immunotherapy within 72 h; anakinra/tocilizumab in FIRES Think autoimmune early in previously healthy young adults.

Tests Glucose, Na, Ca, Mg, urea, liver tests, ammonia, toxicology, antiseizure drug levels, pregnancy (eclampsia) CT then MRI; LP (infection, autoimmune panel, HSV PCR) EEG to confirm cessation and detect non-convulsive SE Common causes Low drug levels/withdrawal, alcohol, stroke, tumour, trauma, infection (HSV), autoimmune, metabolic, eclampsia Treat seizures and search for the cause at the same time.
Quick pearls SAH: nimodipine 60 mg 4-hourly, secure aneurysm  −30, IVIG/PLEX Brain death: prerequisites, apnoea test, ancillary tests Learn one-line management of each neuro emergency.

BTF 4th ed / SIBICC Treat ICP > 22 mmHg; CPP 60–70 mmHg SBP ≥ 100 (50–69 yr) / ≥ 110 (15–49 or > 70) Avoid hypoxia (SpO2 > 94%, PaO2 10–13 kPa), PaCO2 4.5–5 kPa Na 140–145, glucose 6–10, normothermia, Hb > 70 (TRAIN: > 90 better in brain injury) Who needs ICP monitoring GCS 3–8 with abnormal CT, or normal CT + 2 of age > 40, posturing, SBP < 90 Prevent secondary injury: hypoxia, hypotension, hyper/hypocapnia, fever, hyponatraemia.

Tier 0 (all) Head-up 30°, neck neutral, loose ties, sedation/analgesia, normothermia, seizures prophylaxis 7 days (levetiracetam/phenytoin) Tier 1 CPP 60–70, ↑ sedation/analgesia, PaCO2 4.7–5.3 kPa Osmotherapy: mannitol 0.25–1 g/kg or hypertonic saline (Na up to 155, osm < 320) CSF drainage if EVD, EEG Tiers: escalate only when the lower tier fails; go back down when ICP settles.

Tier 2 Mild hypocapnia 4.0–4.5 kPa (with PbtO2/SjvO2 monitoring) Neuromuscular blockade trial MAP challenge to assess autoregulation Repeat CT, consult neurosurgery Tier 3 Barbiturate coma (titrate to burst suppression) Secondary decompressive craniectomy Mild hypothermia 35–36 °C Know what belongs to each tier: examiners ask exactly that.

Hyperventilation ↓ ICP by vasoconstriction but ↓ CBF → ischaemia; avoid PaCO2 DECRA 2011: early bifrontal → worse outcome RESCUEicp 2016: last tier ICP > 25 → ↓ mortality (27 vs 49%) but ↑ vegetative/severe disability Hypothermia Eurotherm3235: ICP-driven hypothermia ↑ unfavourable outcome POLAR: prophylactic hypothermia no benefit Lower ICP ≠ better outcome: the classic exam point.

PbtO2 Target > 20 mmHg; treat hypoxia via FiO2, CPP, PaCO2, Hb, sedation BOOST-II: ↓ time with hypoxia, trend to better outcome; BOOST-3 ongoing/results Microdialysis Lactate/pyruvate ratio > 25–40 = metabolic crisis; glucose, glutamate Others PRx (autoregulation) → CPPopt; SjvO2 55–75%; TCD; continuous EEG; pupillometry Multimodal monitoring personalises CPP and PaCO2 targets.

Points TXA within 3 h in mild-moderate TBI (CRASH-3) No steroids (CRASH: harm) Albumin harmful (SAFE-TBI) VTE prophylaxis after stable CT (24–72 h) Prognosis: IMPACT/CRASH calculators; avoid early withdrawal CRASH-3 for TXA, CRASH for steroids, SAFE-TBI for albumin.

boxes.t: 1. Systematic approach to the comatose overdose
boxes.x: Resuscitate ABC, intubate if GCS ≤ 8 or failing airway; glucose; thiamine ECG early (QRS, QTc, R in aVR, bradyarrhythmia), temperature, pupils Naloxone trial if opioid suspected Assess History (collateral, packets, pill bottles), examination for toxidrome Bloods: paracetamol and salicylate levels in all, ABG, lactate, osmolar gap, CK, U&E, glucose Contact poison centre (TOXBASE) Then Decontamination, enhanced elimination, antidotes, organ support, psychiatric review Resuscitate → ECG → levels → decontaminate → antidote → support.

Activated charcoal 50 g within 1 h of a toxic dose of an adsorbable drug; later for sustained-release or anticholinergic Only with protected airway; contraindicated: hydrocarbons, corrosives, ileus Not for metals, lithium, iron, alcohols Gastric lavage Not routine (AACT/EAPCCT 2013): aspiration, perforation, little benefit Rare: life-threatening amount < 1 h with no antidote (e.g. colchicine) Whole bowel irrigation Body packers, sustained-release, iron, lithium: PEG 1–2 L/h Charcoal yes if early and airway safe; lavage almost never.

Patterns Opioid: coma, miosis, ↓ RR Cholinergic (organophosphates): SLUDGE/DUMBELS, bradycardia, miosis, bronchorrhoea Anticholinergic (TCA, antihistamines): hot, dry, red, mydriasis, tachycardia, retention, delirium Sympathomimetic (cocaine, amphetamine): hyperthermia, sweating, tachycardia, mydriasis Sedative-hypnotic: coma, normal pupils, normal vitals Serotonin: clonus, hyperreflexia, hyperthermia Brady + hypotension + hypothermia β-blocker, CCB, digoxin, clonidine, opioids, sedatives, organophosphate, hypothyroid Pupils, skin, temperature and heart rate sort most toxidromes.

Features Bradycardia, hypotension, AV block; CCB → hyperglycaemia (insulin release blocked); β-blocker → hypoglycaemia; propranolol → seizures, wide QRS Treatment Atropine, fluids, calcium (CaCl 10% 10–20 mL, repeat), glucagon 5–10 mg (β-blocker) High-dose insulin euglycaemia 1 U/kg bolus then 1–10 U/kg/h + dextrose, K monitoring Vasopressors/inotropes (adrenaline), pacing Lipid emulsion 20% 1.5 mL/kg if refractory (lipophilic drug) VA-ECMO for refractory shock; methylene blue for vasoplegia Calcium, high-dose insulin, catecholamines, then ECMO.

Features Nausea, visual (yellow) changes, any arrhythmia (bidirectional VT, AV block with atrial tachycardia), hyperkalaemia in acute toxicity Digoxin-specific Fab Indications: life-threatening arrhythmia, K > 5–6 (acute), level > 10–15 ng/mL (acute) or > 6 (chronic), end-organ damage Dose (vials) = level (ng/mL) × weight (kg) / 100; or 10 vials empirically in acute Avoid Calcium in hyperkalaemia (traditional caution), cardioversion if possible; correct Mg and K Hyperkalaemia in acute digoxin poisoning = give Fab.

Features Na channel block: QRS > 100 ms (seizures), > 160 ms (VT), R in aVR > 3 mm Anticholinergic, α-block hypotension, seizures, coma Treatment Sodium bicarbonate 1–2 mmol/kg boluses to pH 7.45–7.55 and narrow QRS Hyperventilate if intubated; benzodiazepines for seizures (no phenytoin) Noradrenaline for hypotension; lidocaine for VT; lipid emulsion if arrest Avoid class Ia/Ic, flumazenil, physostigmine TCA: bicarbonate and benzodiazepines.

Haemodialysis (EXTRIP) Lithium, salicylate, toxic alcohols, metformin (MALA), valproate, theophylline, barbiturates Urinary alkalinisation Salicylate (urine pH 7.5–8.5); phenobarbital Specific antidotes Paracetamol → NAC; opioids → naloxone; benzodiazepines → flumazenil (rarely); organophosphates → atropine + pralidoxime; cyanide → hydroxocobalamin; CO → O2 / hyperbaric; methaemoglobin → methylene blue Know which poisons are dialysable: "I STUMBLE" / EXTRIP list.

files.title: 10 Ethics, End of Life and Communication

boxes.x: Principles Beneficence: act in the patient's best interests (realistic benefit) Non-maleficence: avoid burdensome treatment without benefit (CPR, ECMO in MOF + dementia) Autonomy: patient's own values via advance directive or surrogate (substituted judgement); families cannot demand inappropriate treatment Justice: fair use of ICU resources In the "do everything" case Respect family role but decision is about the patient's values, not family wishes Explore what "everything" means: fear, guilt, religion, mistrust Apply each principle to the scenario, not as a list of definitions.

Before Quiet room, key family, nurse, senior doctor, interpreter, consistent team message, review facts During (VALUE / SPIKES) Value what family say Acknowledge emotions Listen Understand the patient as a person Elicit questions Ask what they know, give a warning shot, explain prognosis plainly, silence, recommendation After Document, follow-up meeting, support (chaplain, social worker) Evidence Lautrette 2007: VALUE + brochure ↓ PTSD, anxiety, depression in relatives Make a recommendation; do not hand the decision burden to the family.

Definitions (ATS 2015) Futile: cannot achieve its physiological goal (strict, rare; e.g. CPR in refractory MOF) Potentially inappropriate treatment: some chance of effect but competing ethical considerations (burden vs benefit) Time-limited trial: agreed period (e.g. 3–7 days) with defined goals, then reassess Resolving conflict Communication, second opinion, ethics committee, mediation, offer transfer, legal route last Use "potentially inappropriate", not "futile", unless strictly physiological.

Process Consensus and documentation; DNACPR Withdrawing and withholding are ethically equivalent Stop non-comfort measures (bloods, monitoring alarms, feeds as appropriate) Practical Symptom control: opioids and benzodiazepines titrated to distress (double effect; not to hasten death) Vasopressors stopped; terminal extubation or terminal wean; anticipate secretions (glycopyrronium) Family presence, privacy, spiritual support, organ donation referral (DCD) before withdrawal Comfort is the goal; document intent and doses.

Capacity Understand, retain, weigh, communicate; time and decision-specific Without capacity Advance directive, legal proxy, best interests; local legal and religious framework (in Egypt: family-centred decisions, consult hospital ethics/legal) Other topics Brain death diagnosis, organ donation, confidentiality, research consent (deferred), resource allocation, triage State that practice follows local law and institutional policy.

Integrate early Symptom assessment, goals-of-care conversation within 72 h of admission in high-risk patients Triggers: advanced dementia, MOF, prolonged ventilation, poor functional baseline After death Bereavement support, debrief staff, moral distress, Ethicus data on variation Palliative care is active treatment, not abandonment.

files.f: 12 How to Write a 10-Mark SEQ Answer.pdf
files.title: 12 How to Write a 10-Mark SEQ Answer

boxes.x: Split 2 min: read stem twice, underline every task word (discuss, compare, outline, evidence) 1 min: plan headings matching the parts and their marks 13 min: write 2 min: check every part answered, add a summary line Paper level Answer easiest first, never leave a question blank: the first marks of each question are the easiest Stop at 18 min; return if time remains Marks follow the parts: a blank part costs more than a short one.

Seven headings 1. Interpretation: what is going on, severity, numbers 2. Differential: most likely first, life-threatening not to miss 3. Immediate management: ABC, resuscitation, specific first actions 4. Definitive / ongoing care: targets, drugs with doses, monitoring 5. Evidence: trial name + year + one-line result 6. Controversy and emerging: what is debated, what is new 7. Ethics and communication: family, consent, limits of care Use the frame for every scenario: examiners recognise the structure.

Do Headings and short bullet points Numbers and doses (MAP 65, Vt 6 mL/kg PBW, lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg) Name trials with year and result Prioritise: "first …, then …" Answer the exact question asked (if it says compare, use a table) Don't Long prose paragraphs, repeating the stem Lists without explanation for "discuss" Abbreviations without first spelling them out One idea per line; one mark per idea.

Meanings Outline: list main points briefly Describe: what, how, with detail Discuss: points for and against, evidence, conclusion Compare and contrast: similarities and differences, ideally a table Justify / rationale: why, with evidence Evaluate: strengths, weaknesses, verdict The command word tells you how to write the part.

boxes.t: 5. Evidence: how to quote a trial
boxes.x: Template Name (year), population, intervention vs control, main result, limitation e.g. "PROSEVA (2013): severe ARDS P/F < 150, prone ≥ 16 h/day → 28-day mortality 16% vs 33%; experienced centres." When unsure Say the direction of evidence: "large RCTs show no mortality benefit" Quote guidelines: SSC 2021, ESICM 2023, BTF 2016, ATS 2015 Two well-quoted trials beat five vague ones.

First lines "68-year-old diabetic with septic shock from faecal peritonitis: vasopressor-dependent, MAP  40%)." "Immediate priorities run in parallel: airway and oxygen, MAP 65 with noradrenaline, antibiotics within one hour, source control within 6–12 hours." Closing line "Daily review: de-escalate antibiotics, stop steroids when off vasopressors, discuss goals with family." A strong first and last line frame the whole answer.
